## A biomarker that changes its mind

::: columns
::: {.column width="34%"}
In a late-stage oncology trial, one baseline biomarker looked like **nothing**.

A standard survival model scored its effect at ≈ 0.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
sign_flip_fig()
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.15em; margin-top:-.3em;"}
**Harmful early. Protective late.** The two halves cancelled out.
:::

::: notes
OPEN HERE. Do not start with methods. Start with the curve crossing zero.
The point of the whole first act: averaging over time hid a real signal.
Pause after "the two halves cancelled out." That is the hook.

## orthoMTL: don't average over time {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
Cut follow-up into **landmarks**. Fit all of them **at once**, letting each
landmark keep its own effect.

- Survival → a series of yes/no tasks
- One model, not seven
- Oncology application: C-index **0.66 vs 0.63**
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](surv_mtl.png){.fig-fit style="--fig-h:380px;" fig-alt="Diagram converting survival times into a sequence of binary classification tasks, one per landmark."}
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.25em; margin-top:.3em;"}
**`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`** — on CRAN, 2026
:::

::: notes
This is the promotion slide. 45 seconds, no more. The sell is: if your outcome is
time-to-event and you suspect effects change over time, this package will show you that.
Vervier 2014 (method), Juric 2026 Annals of Oncology (application).
:::

## From PhD code to CRAN

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Twelve-year-old research code. An agent did the packaging work.

::: {.fragment}
It also found a **real bug** in my own 2014 gradient — labels were $\pm1$,
the code used the $0/1$ formula.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.4em;"}
Caught because flipping every label **must** flip the answer. It didn't.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](cran.png){.fig-fit style="--fig-h:200px;" fig-alt="CRAN logo."}
:::
:::

::: notes
Keep this tight. The transferable idea is the symmetry check, not the bug.
Say: "the agent cannot invent that check — I had to know the maths. But it ran it."
:::

## Then CRAN rejected us. Twice. {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.5em; line-height:1.9; margin-top:.5em;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** An invalid `LICENSE` field.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**2.** A hard-coded `set.seed()`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.7em; color:#FF4E00;"}
Neither was caught by any automated check. Both were caught by **a human**.
:::

::: notes
Deliberately dark slide, big type, slow delivery. This is the pivot from act one to act two.
Both rejections cost round-trips measured in weeks of calendar time.
:::

## So: would a "skill file" have saved me?

::: {style="font-size:1.1em;"}
Skill files are everywhere. **Does anyone measure them?**
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
Re-break the package with four classic CRAN defects. Hand it to an agent under
**six conditions**. Frozen prompt, fresh copy each time, results **blinded** before scoring.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: "78%"
design_fig()
```

::: notes
A4 is the cheat arm: I wrote it FROM this package's own rejection history. It should win.
Flag that now so the result lands harder.
:::

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:.2em;"}
::: {style="font-size:6.5em; font-weight:700; color:#FF4E00; line-height:1;"}
0
:::
::: {style="font-size:1.4em; margin-top:.2em;"}
difference between the best skill file and **no skill file at all**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.05em; margin-top:.8em;"}
All **`r n_seed`/`r n_runs`** runs fixed all four defects — including the control.
Even the arm I wrote from our own failures.

## Why the control did so well

::: {style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.4em;"}
::: {.fragment}
The agent runs **`R CMD check`** and reads its own failures.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em;"}
A machine oracle beats any checklist — it **can't be out of date**.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.5em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Skill files add nothing where a tool already tells the truth.
:::
:::

::: notes
This is the mechanistic explanation and the most useful thing on the slide deck.
Where R CMD check is silent — the LICENSE field, the seed — nothing saved us either.
:::

## What I am *not* claiming {.smaller}

- Every arm could read the CRAN docs anyway → "**no benefit beyond docs at hand**", not "skills are useless"
- **One** package, **one** agent, **one** model version
- I extended the sample size **after** peeking — post-hoc, not pre-registered
- No positive control, so I can't prove the measurement *could* detect a win
- 3 runs lost to rate limits (`r n_runs` of 60 analysed)

::: notes
Say these out loud and quickly. Credibility is the currency of a null result.
Do not skip the peeking admission.
:::

## Take home {background-color="#F5F5F5"}

::: {style="font-size:1.2em; line-height:1.7;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** If effects can change over time, don't average them away → `orthoMTL`
:::
::: {.fragment}
**2.** Agents are good at checks a **machine** can run. Buy those, not checklists.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**3.** The hard bugs needed **me** to know which symmetry had to hold.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.8em; text-align:center; font-size:1.1em; color:#FF4E00;"}
Generation got cheap. Verification did not.
:::

::: {style="font-size:.6em; margin-top:.5em; text-align:center;"}
`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL` · Vervier et al. 2014 · Juric et al. 2026
:::

# Backup {.unnumbered}

## Backup: what the six arms were

| Arm | Skill file |
|---|---|
| A0 | none (control) |
| A1 | CRAN checklist |
| A2 | CRAN process + adversarial review |
| A3 | general R-package development |
| A4 | written from *this* package's failures |
| A5 | raw handbook text |

## Backup: the three ways we checked correctness {.smaller}

| Check | What it proves |
|:--|:--|
| Against the old validated package | identical coefficients on 5 fixed cases |
| Flip every label | answer must flip; `0.62` → `0.000` |
| Simulated data, known truth | recovers the right features, 10/10 seeds |

::: notes
The survival path is exactly where comparing against the old code cannot reach —
there was no old survival code. That is why the simulation oracle exists.
:::

## Backup: what I would change

- Seed defects only a **human reviewer** could catch
- Add a deliberately handicapped arm as a positive control
- Judge each package several times, not once
- More packages, more models
